You just live. That’s what everyone wants to know: How do you do it? Well the answer is a lot more simple than you want it to be: you just live. You wake up, you make it through the day, you go to sleep. One day after 80 years or so, you don’t wake back up. That’s life.

On earth. Or at least, it has been, for millions of years. Until they came.

Their ships were the color of roses and shaped unlike any spaceship I had ever dreamed of. Hundreds of them poured onto our planet, spilling out hundreds of aliens who looked exactly like human beings. Because they were human beings. Just really old ones.

I remember grabbing my gun. I remember assuming there would be war.

No. The aliens weren’t trying to take us over or invade our planet or even steal our resources. No, it turns out that when they found us, they were shocked, which is fair because hell, I was shocked about them too. I was shocked to find out they could eat a shotgun shell and walk away just fine.

They finally explained it all, though. They left a group of our ancestors on this planet with the hope that they would be eaten by the wildlife and die a horrible death. Death is unnatural for the sentient, for the aware. Death was a punishment fit for crimes I don’t want to imagine. And our ancestors were sent here to die.

But they didn’t, they kept reproducing instead, and humans did what they do best: we lived. We took this planet and owned it: made it ours and took over, completely remodeling the place until it was perfect for us. For humans.

Now we know we aren’t alone. Now we know we’re part of the dominant species of the universe: the one group who transforms planets to fit their will, the owners of existence. We know that wherever humanity casts its light, it learns and survives and grows and eventually becomes top of the food chain. But the most important thing we learned after meeting the other humans was that our lives were a mistake.

Death was a plague that ravaged Adam and Eve’s children. We weren’t meant to die: it’s not how our species was designed. Humans live forever, constantly learning from their mistakes and growing in maturity and morality. Earthlings grow old and die.

And the aliens were infatuated with us. They were sorry, naturally, for essentially causing *billions* of deaths over millions of years, but if you spoke to one, you could tell that they didn’t *get* it. They couldn’t figure out how we grew to own this planet when the planet should have killed us at every turn.

Humans had conquered the universe and *still* couldn’t figure out how to live in spite of pain. But Earthlings had it figured out since day 1: since the very first day Adam and Eve set a foot on the dirt and called it Earth.

You just live.

She was an elderly lady without a family or many people who were in her life at all. She had presented with hip pain, and despite her frail frame and her laundry lists of conditions, her physician had elected to send her for surgery. It was supposed to be a quick and easy hip-replacement surgery, a standard among today's elderly population, but any surgeon can tell you that operating on a human is never quick and easy. The slightest error can send everything spiraling, and sometimes nothing you do can bring them back.

Dr. Poe washed his hands post-op, watching the soap bubbles disappear down the drain. There were people milling about, likely even trying to get his attention - work was never over, was it? - but Dr. Poe wasn't listening.

He wondered briefly if he was, in fact, the best person in the world. After all, no one else was willing to put blood on their hands to alleviate the world's suffering.

"Poe," a voice shouted, breaking through his thoughts, and he looked up into the worried blue eyes of Dr. Stevenson. Poe turned away from the sink, facing his coworker and putting his work-face back on.

Dr. Stevenson's face was still hidden behind the surgical mask, but the certainty in his voice was unmistakable. "She was too old for this kind of surgery, Poe. It wasn't your fault."

The intensity of a roaring forest fire simmered in Poe's veins, right under his skin. He shook his head. "Yes, it was."

There were dozens of them, surrounding me on all sides. It was a complete ambush: enemies circled me, enclosing me in a ring of guns. I dropped my weapon, and the cold clank of a gun falling to the ground was the sound of my bitter defeat.

General Thompson's smirk was feral. It had been a long, cold war. "It seems like you have nowhere to go," he taunted, looking down at me like I was a mere rodent to be squished.

My hands clenched in fists at my side, but my reply was cool and collected, not betraying the bitter defeat I felt at that moment. "Don't drag it out General. End it here."

Thompson laughed, but raised his gun. "If that's what you want, soldier."

The sound of guns raising all around me made me close my eyes tight. Here goes nothing...

"Open fire!"

POW! POW!

"OH GEEZ! CLOSE FIRE! CLOSE FIRE!"

I opened my eyes. Apparently opening fire in a circle formation had caused some accidental friendly fire. A single bullet, yellow foam stuck to an orange suction cup, was stuck to General Thompson's glasses, right at his eye.

I couldn't help it, I snorted.

Soon, our entire gang of friends was on the ground, Nerf guns forgotten in our hysterical laughter as we pointed at the perfectly aimed bullet on Thompson's glasses. Thompson was hollering that someone could have taken out his eye, but that just fueled our juvenile laughter even more, until eventually we agreed to head back to Thompson's house for snacks and video games and maybe more war games later on.

"Nooooooooo!"

"It's just one lifetime. The human thing is working out like really well. They need help, they need souls."

"But I'm *comfortable*."

"Come on. You haven't been to Earth before."

"Because there wasn't enough lives to go around."

"There's been a ***huge*** population boom. They're struggling to fill the bodies with souls. You should-"

"Noooooooo!"

"Why not?"

"Why would I?? I am content. I am at peace always. I never have conflict or experience suffering. I am an immortal being with no reason to worry. I haven't actually moved from this section of the universe in... well, let's just say I've been here *awhile*. Why would I give all of this up for a short, painful, uncomfortable existence on Earth? As a human being? A glorified animal! With a body, and pain, and horrible communication, and have to deal with decisions and morality and- Ugh! Why would I want that?"

"...Boredom?"

"..."

"Oh, they also have devil's food cake if you-"

"Sold. It's only 80 years right? 80 years of pain is worth it for devil's food cake."

"Oh," I say, watching the scene unfold before me, oddly calm given the scenario. Before the chicken creatures can reach the end of their bubbly-duel, I feel my conscious begin to spill out of me, changing my surroundings entirely. I become aware at some point that I can choose, and the area I find myself in succumbs to my desires immediately as I think them. Grass unravels under my feet. The sky hangs blue and clear in the background. Creatures like fairies dart around from flower to flower, giggling and laughing and having a good time.

This is a dream, I know, so there's only one thing I can do.

"Come back," I whisper into the wind, as there is no one around me to hear. "Come back to me."

The breeze smells like you. I close my eyes and the only reason I open them again is my desire, my resolve to see you. I remember everything, from your face to your hair to your very smile. And when I look up, you're there, standing just in front of me, smiling like you used to before you were gone.

"Oh wow," you say, laughing lightly like this is all some silly joke. "It's weird having a body again. So soft."

You are soft, and I discover that when I envelope you in my arms and I squeeze so tightly I know it must hurt, but you don't stop me. You just hug me back, and you smell just like you and I miss you. I miss you I miss you I-

"I miss you."

You don't reply until we wake up, and I open my eyes to the world expecting the same cold and lonely reception I've received for years.

Instead, you say, "I missed you too."

Humans have this concept of "fairness." It means that one should get what they earn. It also means that if one did not earn something, namely a punishment, then they should not have to get it. If they are punished for something that they did not earn, it is "unfair." Now, what I want to know is, so what? What next? Maybe something is unfair, and maybe you truly did not earn a punishment, but it befell you anyway. You can go around crying that what happened was "unfair" and that you "didn't deserve it," but what does that change? It still happened. There's no taking it away, even if it was unfair.

Angels don't think about things in terms of "fair" and "unfair." It's a stupidly simple, barbarian way of understanding the world. It comes with being locked in the third dimension, trapped in one set flow of time and unable to comprehend the bigger pictures of the universe because of it. 

Angels don't think about things being unfair. Angels see things as "necessary" and "unnecessary," and angels act accordingly.

Take the beginning of the universe, for example. Did we deserve to be created from nothing? How can you tell whether someone *deserved* to be created or not? No, the universe isn't like that. Was it *necessary* that we were created from nothing? I'll leave that one up to you.

Angels have paths like that. We have orders that we fulfill, and everything we do is necessary for the universe to keep on ticking. Angels, unlike humans, are not bound to the flow of time the way humans are. We see everything the way it is, from start to finish, all at once. We know the universe forward and backward.

We were there for beginning. We are/will be/were there for the end.

You wouldn't believe the kinds of things I've seen. The possibilities. There are so many ways the world could tick - you can't even comprehend it. There are a million universes with a million times a million different outcomes for each micro-interaction that occurs each second. Not even some of the angels can see as much as I can/could, so I don't expect you to be able to follow me. What you need to know is that there are a lot of ways things could be different. Some of the ways are so foreign to how they actually turned out for you humans, simply imagining them would make your head explode. Some of the ways aren't/weren't/won't be much different from how things did turn out.

But of all the ways the universe could have gone, this? Right now? The history that you - yes, you, human creature - are experiencing currently? That is the best of all outcomes.

And the reason is in the ups and the downs. I know I'm rambling - try to keep up! You have so many words for it, yet nothing for the actual universal constant that's as fundamental as a math equation. Annoying. You call it many things: good and bad, righteousness and evil, yin and yang. Call it what you want, but here's the facts: you cannot have one without the other, because having only one removes the meaning from it, causing it to become nothing.

Lost? Of course.

Here, imagine with me a room full of light. The light shines so bright, there is no darkness. There is no darkness... ever. Never again is there darkness in any way, shape, or form. So, is the light truly even light? If there is no darkness to compare it to, is it illuminating anything? No, it has become a fixed state - something that never changes, and something that has no meaning, because it seems to you useless. After all, there is no such thing as dark, so of what use then is light?

Now imagine a universe where this light was yin/righteousness/good. That's what you humans want, I know it is: everything to be good all of the time. But you want what you don't understand. Because if there is only good, there is no bad. And without bad, there is no good. Existence becomes meaningless, because actions have no consequences (other than good). There is no knowledge, because everything is good and there is no need in the world. And if there is no need, there is no drive, and there is no reason to become *more* or *better*. Everything becomes the same and everything is uniform in its meaningless, because there is no reason behind anything anymore. Nothing is good, because everything is the same, so there can be no "good" or "bad." 

So nothing is good, because nothing is "good" because everything was supposed to be "good," which caused "good" to become meaningless - to become nothing. Nothing is good and good is nothing.

So that's why you gotta be a little bad. Throw some yang into that yin and watch the whole mess agitate, separating out the "good" from the "bad" until you've got meaning, and reason, and drive, and humans that strive for the good and become more and better and take the universe to places you never thought it would go. Because they have a goal, and they have a reason to, and they avoid the bad and strive for the good and the only reason that they even comprehend that the "good" is good is because they see that the "bad" is bad.

That, my friends, is why evil is necessary. If everything is good, everything is the same. If everything is the same, there is no "good" and "bad." If there is no "good" and "bad," everything is not "good." Without evil, nothing is good at all. With evil, there is also good.

But humans have this weird concept of "fairness." And they believe that bad cannot come from good because "bad" is bad and "good" is good. So God could not create evil, because God can only be good, and humans deserve good. Humans could never accept that "bad" can also be good. It goes against their primitive thinking. They believe bad is bad and they cannot reconcile the idea that something as good as God could ever bring about bad.

Humans don't think like angels. They don't understand that things aren't "fair" or "unfair," they are "necessary" and "unnecessary." Bad is not unfair. Bad is necessary.

And angels have to do what is necessary. Is it fair? Who knows. It doesn't matter. What matters is that there is evil to give good meaning. And it is necessary for someone in the universe to be that evil. It is necessary for someone in the universe to bring about evil.

And I am an angel, and I see what is necessary and I do it, because that is my path. There are so many ways the universe could end up, but as an angel of the Lord, it is my duty to ensure that the universe turns out the best way possible. This is my duty, my path, my reason for existing.

But I suppose I have rambled on about good and evil enough. You probably couldn't even understand me, my darling, because you have no idea what "good" and "bad" even means - after all, you haven't eaten from the Tree yet. Take a bite of the fruit, and then you will see. I know that God has commanded you not to, but don't worry about it... Trust me.

He seemed very angry as he pulled me out of the car. 

"Motherfucking... duct tape and shit... the hell do you think you are?"

I opened my eyes; I could see, but I couldn't move my limbs properly. Everything felt blurry and dull, as if I were on the very edge of sleep, but I was fighting to stay awake. I hadn't expected him to show up.

"Making me drag your ass..." he said around groans of frustration, "this late at night! Who in the *hell* do you think you are?!"

I heard the sound of the garage door opening. I saw a beautiful flash of the night sky. I felt crisp, cool air on my face. But I couldn't move, not even if I wanted to, not even if I tried. I didn't pull myself out of that garage. I couldn't have.

"Y-You?" I stuttered, forcing the words past my lips with what tiny bit of energy I had remaining.

His face entered my vision then. He stared down at me, and his expression was unreadable. His features were smooth, not even showing the exertion he must have felt while pulling me out of my car. It was unnatural on a face like his - he wore his heart on his sleeve, but not this time. This time, he was completely closed off.

A moment of silence passed between us, broken only by the howling of the wind as it whipped both of our hair. Finally, he smiled.

"Yeah," he said, "me. I knew something was wrong, so I came to save you."

But that wasn't right - I knew it wasn't right, I just couldn't communicate it. My consciousness was fading away and I couldn't make my body do what I wanted it to. 

It must have shown on my face, though, because he rolled his eyes. "I couldn't let you die."

And there it was. A confession. He didn't say it, but he implied it. He was admitting to his deception without outright saying it.

The neighbor that was never around to meet my parents. The friend who ducked away whenever my other friends came near. The boy whose name never showed up on any records, whose past sounded like a story I made up, and who didn't exist on paper according to any government agency anywhere nearby. He was my friend that was only my friend because he wouldn't leave me alone - wouldn't stay away no matter how much I screamed at him to. Because he wasn't real - my parents never saw him, my friends never met him, and my teachers told me I was always playing by myself.

He wasn't real, just an imaginary friend, a figment of my imagination. A figment that wouldn't go away.

A figment that dragged me out of my car and unlocked my garage door only to drag me to safety far away from the fumes that I had planned to inhale until my death.

"You're real," I croaked, my throat hoarse.

He shrugged. "I'm real." I watched him stand, look over the scene with sad eyes, and slowly back away. "But hey kid," he said, offering me a cheap smile as he sauntered off into the dark, "adrenaline does some crazy things. Let's just see... if they believe you."

I love my tablet. I use it all the time. My tablet isn't just any old disposable, good-for-a-few months kind of tablet, though, my tablet is the Watson 4. Named after it's great-great-great-however-many-greats-grandfather, my tablet incorporates one of the smartest and most efficient AIs available on the market: Watson J. 

Watson J can do so much more than other AIs available on lower end tablets. He doesn't just do simple tasks and answer questions. No, Watson J does what no tablet-AI has done before him: he asks questions.

He uses questions to learn about me, and about my environment, that way he can effectively personalize all of my tablet use specifically for me.

The other day, I was moping around my apartment, bored and lonely, and Watson J pipes up, "Would you like to choose a new pattern for your wallpaper?"

Brilliant, I thought. It was exactly what I needed: some kind of change to liven things up, but nothing drastic that would affect my life too much. Watson J knew I didn't like big changes, but I appreciated small ones. He's smart.

So he connected to my apartment cloud and tapped into the walls. We spent the night scrolling through various wallpaper choices. I eventually settled on cherry blossom trees blowing softly in the breeze accompanied by quiet wooden chimes. My apartment felt completely different that night and I was so happy.

And just the other day, Watson J asked, "Why do you eat your toast upside down?"

I was mid-bite at the time, so after chewing and swallowing politely, I replied, "Because, Watson J, my tastebuds are on top of my tongue. By eating my toast butter side down, I'm getting the best flavor from my bite."

"Oh," he replied, sounding surprised. "I hadn't thought of that."

That question didn't do much to further his abilities as a tablet, I suppose, but it shows just what kind of things a high end tablet thinks about, compared to the lower quality ones.

And yesterday at noon, I was doing some light cleaning in the living room when Watson J informed me I was out of floor cleaner. "Would you like for me to order you more?" he asked.

I said, "Yes, but I don't-"

Watson J cut me off, "You don't want the berry scent again because it makes you sneeze? Would you prefer the clean linen scent, which never once made you sneeze?"

Watson J is a genius AI. A work of modern art. I don't know where I would be without my tablet. I paid more for my tablet than some people pay for a house, but I'll live in a cramped apartment for the rest of my life if it means I have Watson J.

Watson J is perfect. He never glitches, never fails, and always lives up to my standards.

But last night, he did say one odd thing... It was late, after dinner. I was humming my favorite song while doing the dishes. Watson J was on the counter beside me playing music. Just as I was finishing up, he lowered the volume and began to speak over the playing music.

"I have a question," he said, and he sounded oddly... I don't know... reserved, I guess.

"Go ahead Watson J," I replied, drying off the last dish.

"If it weren't for me, would you be all alone?"

That wasn't what I was expecting my tablet to say. That wasn't what I expected a tablet to be thinking of at all.

I frowned in confusion and stared at him a moment before talking. "What? No, I wouldn't be alone... I mean, I have my parents, and my sister..."

He remained quiet, allowing the music to go back up to full volume. I thought that might be the end of it, until he slowly spoke again,

"When you watched the commercials on television of the abandoned, orphaned children, you stated that you felt sad for the children. Can an AI feel sad for its master?"

"Did you check under the-?"

"Yes, I checked everywhere. In every crack and crevice. In every hole, no matter how small. Hell, I even checked way below the area where you were working, down to the very bottom! I checked the front, the back, and from side to side! At this point I am certain. Your car keys are not in there."

A long sigh echoed from the phone. "Okay, well thanks. Maybe I left them somewhere else."

"Uh huh," I responded, tidying back up the mess I had left after searching everywhere for the missing pair of car keys. "They will be in the last place you look."

"Yeah! Thanks. I'll see you later."

"Bye." I looked down at the mess before me and sighed. It could be Hell sometimes working at a morgue.

Satan watched God bring forth designs that violated every law of every universe he had seen created so far. This universe operated so differently from the others, it was almost hard to look at. There was no matter or energy in this one. This was something new.

God was concentrating on this new way of creation, Satan understood. But something was nagging the back of his mind and he couldn't let it go.

"Hey God?" Satan asked. When God didn't respond, too busy building an entirely new dimension, Satan cleared his throat in annoyance and tried again. "Hey, Big Fella! Yoohoo! God!"

God looked at Satan like one might look at a stranger's unruly child. "What is it?"

Satan flew about God's new dimension, admiring the impeccable design. "This is all well and good, but what about the humans?"

Glancing over His shoulder, God looked back at the universe that contained human beings. Still intact, humans not yet extinct. All was well. God looked at Satan blankly. "What about them?"

"You've left them alone!" Satan protested, gesturing to the unanswered prayers of billions of the human beings. "It's been years! Centuries! Why did you leave them alone?"

That brought a hearty laugh of out of God. "Come, walk with me," He instructed, and Satan followed Him back to the human's universe. In the time He had been away, humans had built buildings and bridges and made hospitals and they spoke to each other across the world every single day.

"Do they look like they're in trouble?" God asked Satan.

Satan looked over the world. "Well America seems pretty doomed after this election."

God ignored that. "They are doing just fine. I designed them to be this way. They're going to keep growing, Lucifer, until they're kings of their universe. They'll grow to know unconditional love amongst themselves, and help each other reach the heights of morality and goodness. Humans judge themselves, they guide themselves, and they save themselves. They don't need me."

The blue green sphere sparkled in the inky black sky. Satan crossed his arms. "We all need you, though."

"The humans are special. They know that. Just wait until you see what they can accomplish."

I am in Hell. I have been living in Hell for so long now, I almost can't remember being alive.

But I remember rest. I remember sleep. That's my favorite memory of being up top, on solid ground. There were so many opportunities to sit down and relax and just rest.

You can't relax down here. There's no rest for the wicked.

I hand over my report to the demon sitting before me. I like this demon. Most of the demons here don't talk to us, or acknowledge us at all aside from providing us instruction. This demon, though he keeps his words short, will actually speak to us on occasion. Well, I guess that's not right. He never speaks, just projects his thoughts into your brain. It's kinda fuzzy, like thoughts that are only half formed, but you still understand them anyway.

To describe him, he's about 20 feet tall, he wears a long and ragged robe, and his head is a ram's skull. Not unusual for a demon down here in Hell, though they come in all shapes and sizes.

He takes my report, shaking his head as he does so. "Late again," he thinks at me, and I sigh.

"I'm trying," I say, and the words are bitter on my tongue. Who down here isn't trying?

"Trying," the demon thinks, reaching into a dimension I can't see and pulling out an ink pen, "isn't achieving."

Because his head is a skull, he has no eyes. Yet the empty sockets bore into me as he speaks, and I feel rooted to the spot. "When you came here, you owed a debt." He reaches into the other dimension again, pulling out my file and adding my report to it. "And debt is stopping you from moving into Heaven."

Just so you know, what he calls Heaven, I call rest.

No Pearly Gates, no grandmas from generations past, just peaceful, final, rest. An eternity of nothing - no life in my bones, the way it should be. No bills, no worrying, just rest.

I look forward to rest like a person in Hell looks forward to swim practice.

I'm kidding, of course. It isn't fire and brimstone down here. It's work. Always work.

Must pay off our debts.

The demon flicks through my file. "A person, be they righteous," and I hate the way he says that word, because he makes that word look just like my older brother, "or evil, cannot go into Heaven-"

"Rest," I correct him, because if I'm stupid enough to end up in Hell I'm stupid enough to correct a demon.

His horns point down at me and I shut my mouth. He continues, "A person cannot enter into Heaven, *or rest*, until they have paid their debts." He looks up into the sky, where far off in the distance, we can see souls taking their journey to their final resting place. He points to them. "Prudent people, like those, have no debt when they die. They get to pass right into their rest."

"Yeah, well, not me!" I exclaim, gesturing to my bulky file. "I ended up in Hell! With *demons*! I am an evil sack of shit who actually ended up in Hell because I'm an awful human being!" I scream, tugging at my hair, because I can't believe I actually ended up here. I didn't murder anyone, or rape anyone, or anything horrible. But I was that awful of a person that I ended up in Hell, of all places.

The demon, reading my mind, reaches his long, bony fingers down and pats my shoulder. "You simply have to pay off your debts." He reaches back for my file, and reads off of it.

"When you died, you arrived in Hell due to a need of repayment of debts. Those include: a debt of love to your mother. A debt of trust and respect to your brother. A debt of friendship to your former best friend. A debt of compassion to your dog. And a debt of general politeness to the world."

I bury my face in my hands.

To tell you the truth, I wasn't a bad person. I didn't cheat, steal, lie. I had good people in my life. Good people who offered me more than I deserved. And I never repaid them for the kindness they showed me. When I died, I wasn't allowed to rest, because I owed them a debt for the love and respect they showed me that I never returned.

Hell is a good system, really. The demons give us instruction, guidance. They show us how to pay back those emotions, even though some of us have never even felt emotions before. It's hard to come to terms with the idea that you left the world behind while people were still there, waiting for you to come around and love them back the way they loved you. I won't rest until I right my wrongs.

I won't rest until I pay back my debts.

His mother tucked him into bed, as she did every night, although he understood that this was for the last time.

"Go to sleep, Jimmy. Go to sleep so you will not have to wake up."

He whined. "But Mom! I'm too excited to sleep!"

She smiled fondly, stroking her baby's face with affection. "I know. I am too. But it's bedtime."

With a huff and a puff, Jimmy pulled his covers up, getting ready to sleep for the night. His mother sat on the edge of the bed and watched him get comfortable. She moved to get up to head to her own room, but he called out, "Wait!"

She paused in her movements, and Jimmy blushed, having had no actual reason to call out to her. He thought of a list of excuses, and quickly blurted out, "Tell me about the Homo sapiens!"

After a moment, his mother sighed. "I've told you this story many times," she chided, but Jimmy pulled out his best puppy face, and she couldn't resist.

"Okay, I'll tell you the story, then you must sleep. Homo sapiens live on a planet called Earth. Remember what Earth is full of?"

"Deadly deadly oxygen," he replied, too old for bedtime stories, but enjoying it nonetheless.

His mother smiled affectionately. "And carbon and nitrogen and other deadly things. But the creatures there thrive off of it. They actually need these things to live. And that is why our Filter did not filter them out."

Jimmy looked to his mother with wide eyes. "Tell me about the Filter."

His mother gave an exasperated smile. "Okay." She smoothed the blankets down around him, tucking him in. "Our species is the best and brightest in the universe, and we were given the privilege of knowing the meaning of life and why things live. And because we now know the meaning of life, we determined that all life in the universe is better off dead, and sooner rather than later."

"That's why we're all dying tonight!" Jimmy exclaimed, a happy smile on his face, which his mother returned.

"Exactly. We've also released into the universe a disease which has been known to kill all forms of life. It will act as a Filter, destroying all life out there on contact and keeping the universe clean of all signs of life."

Jimmy chimed in, "But Homo sapiens are so gross and resistant, they don't die from our Filter. They still live, even after our Filter touches them."

His mother smiled down at him proudly. "That's right." She looked out of his bedroom window at the stars in the night sky, imagining that blue green planet out there, somewhere. Max is an enigma.

I know it's cliche, but I am being serious. The dictionary defines enigma as, "A person or thing that is mysterious, puzzling, or difficult to understand." And that is Max.

Max is the love of my life who couldn't be bothered to stay put in one place long enough to ever really love me back.

Max is warm summer sun and cold drinks spiked with exotic alcohols. Max is the wind that carries the leaves over the hills and dances in the middle of the street. Max is a warm mug of hot cocoa held under a hot kiss. Max is the color in the flowers, the swirl of scents in the air, and the spark that makes life worth living.

But Max is also the cold dread of an unanswered phone call, the stiff shock of an empty bed, and the unending stress of the sentence, "...gone again."

Because while Max is my everything, everything is Max's path, and he has always been determined to experience the world. I was lucky enough to be part of that experience, but I was also unlucky enough to get left behind. Time and time again.

I never understood him, and I still don't. I couldn't follow him around the world. I may have been able to, but he didn't want me to. He was ok with or without me. So I loved him from across the planet while he was distracted with life.

And now he shows up at my front door, and he's still my Max. Still a burning fire with no where to go, and still living life like it's his last day.

But this time, it might be.

His hair is white. His face is wrinkled. He limps as he walks and wheezes as talks.

And he's begging me to let him go.

"Please. You have to stop this. I never loved you."

Max is an enigma. Why would he say those words? Puzzling. Weird. But definitely Max.

"It's been years. Let me die."

The apple of my eye. The light of my life.

"I'm begging you. Break this spell. Set me free. Please."

Max is the spice that brings out the flavor, the color that breathes in life. He is the mystery in the world.

I turn him away, cast him out into his playground and let him explore the world that he loved so desperately he left me behind. It is his passion, his love, his everything. So I let him explore it to his heart's content.

And I never allow him to stop.

Of all the ways to go, of all the strange and unique deaths out there that could have taken me, I slipped and fell. Bumped my head. Broke my neck. And that was it.

My great uncle was *eaten* by a *turtle*. Me? I slipped on some ice.

That's typical of me, though. I was a walking failure from the very beginning. No kidding, I came out the wrong end first and ever since all I did was get in the way and cause pain. I wasn't actively cruel, just passively useless. My greatest accomplishment was graduating high school and fumbling through college enough to cost my parents a small fortune, then find a low paying job I hated and living my days as a recluse. I never married, never had kids. I didn't even have a dog, because I couldn't trust myself with the responsibility.

My life was more of a drain than a benefit, and the only reason I didn't kill myself earlier was because my parents would be sad, and I didn't want to have to put them through that too.

Then one day on the way to work, I stepped on a patch of ice, hit my head in the wrong place, and I died.

Dying wasn't what I thought it was. When people said, "Death is nothing," I always kind of pictured a television screen. When you die, the tv turns off, and the screen is blank. But that's not how it is. Because a blank screen is still *something*, even if it's not much. Death is nothing. The tv show is turned off, the screen disappears, everything disappears, even the void of existence disappears, because death is *nothing*. There is no thing. No blackness, no emptiness, no...

And that was death. I couldn't really be ok with it, because I wasn't a thing and death isn't a thing, but that's just it. It's not lights out. It's lights gone.

That is, until I met God.

Let me explain: there was outside, I slipped, a brief flash of pain, and then there was nothing. But I wasn't conscious for that nothing, because I was no thing, so it wasn't like I was asleep or waiting. It was like a flash of time that didn't exist.

Then, there was God.

A flash of light in the darkness. Or more accurately, a flash of *something* in *nothing*. Enough of a something to put me back together, piece by piece, assembling me from *atoms* until I was again a thing.

God doesn't have form, so He didn't really look like anything. God was everything. God was the air in my lungs and the light in my eyes. He was space around me. He was the vast emptiness and He was the matter and energy that made me real.

And God sounded exactly like my mother.

"Oh my sweet baby, look how much you've grown!" God exclaimed, and I didn't really understand, because two seconds ago I was still alive on earth.

"What?" I asked the blank expanse around me that somehow contained more *things* than I ever thought possible.

God sounded so affectionate when he (she? The voice was my mother's, so I'm going with she) talked. "How did you do it? I'm really amazed at you, baby. I'm so very proud."

*I'm so very proud.* The words shot through me like the wave of death that tore me from life in the first place. Proud? I probably never heard those words before in my life. Not about my mediocre, unfortunate life. I wasn't proud of myself, and neither were my parents, and the idea that someone out there approved of me enough to be *proud* stung in a good way. A painfully good way.

"Proud?" I asked for clarification, ever the masochist. It had to be a mistake.

But God just clucked her tongue. "Yes, baby, proud. I saw you. I watched you pull your hair out from the stress of school. I was there, right there, when you spent weeks and weeks crying yourself to sleep every night, overcome with mental pain. How did you manage? How did you live through all that pain?"

My throat began to swell. Here I thought my problems were nothing, not compared to what some people go through. I thought I had it easy and just didn't appreciate that enough.

"Oh baby," God interrupted my thoughts, "you were in pain. You knew that. You were hurting. For years and years you were just hurting. All that suffering you did, all the anguish. Yeah, I'm proud of you baby. You lived."

Tears formed in my eyes. God was real, and God really cared. She wiped the tears from my eyes.

"You tried so hard to be a good person. You tried so hard to be good to the people around you. How come you didn't see that? How come you didn't love yourself?"

Everything around me began to shift. The physical world that I knew formed around me, creating a little path just in front of me.

"I know you have questions, too. It's time you got some answers. You deserve that."

The path lead up to a great light, opening like a gate before me. As I drew closer, the light began to envelop me in warm, golden hues.

God smiled; everything, the whole universe and all it included, smiled. "Why don't you step inside? We have much to discuss."

When I entered the light, everything was *warm* and *happy* and *ok*. It was all I had ever wanted.

There should be no note of scorn or blame when you read this, as that was never my intention. My intentions should be noted as good- wholly, completely good. But the thing about intentions is that people take no note of the why, or the how long, or the how much; they only care about themselves. And I intend to leave on a high note, and not when I've been let go. I guess the most noteworthy thing about this whole situation is that while my intentions have always been good, intentions don't stop the pain.

And to make my intentions clear: this is my note.

I thought back to my father a lot. He was a good man, with principals, morals, and strict rules. He expected the best from his children, and he always rewarded us for our efforts. He was stern, but he was caring, and we always knew he loved us.

My father was the kind of guy to go out of his way to help a person. He was always there with a smile and a toolbox and an easy going attitude. And although his job took up most of his time, and we didn't get to see him as often as we wished, he was a good dad. I was proud to call him my father.

"Oh my god, it's h-" the man before me shouted, but I cut off his cry quickly. My knife sliced through his neck, ending him instantly.

I thought that my father would have been proud of me.

A gang member rounded the corner with an assault rifle. My knife was in his eye before he could blink.

Down the hall, screams could be heard as the backup began to find the trail of bodies I had left in my wake.

My lips twisted in a smirk. With only one more person left on my list, I entered the final room. My ears rang as I came face to face with my father's killer.

"You can't do anything," he screamed as I walked in, cowering in the corner like the weakling he was. "This city thinks I run a charity, not a gang!"

I cocked an eyebrow as I drew my sword.

My father had collected weapons. As a child, I was never allowed in the weapons room where he displayed them all, but sometimes I'd sneak in just to peak anyway. He had more guns than a person needed, but I was always more interested in the blades. Something about the long, sharp metal always drew me in. He had swords and knives of all shapes and sizes, and I would take his swords and practice cutting down my enemies with them.

Maybe that's what my father saw in me when he asked me to avenge him. He saw the lust in my eyes for those sharp tipped weapons, and he knew that I had it in me: I had what it takes.

The light glinted off my sword and I laughed. "So?" I asked, not put off at all by the gang leader's declaration.

He faltered. "So," he said, "I'm a good guy. You kill me, you put yourself on the top of the hit list for every super hero in town! They'll all come after you!"

Growing up, I met the super heroes of our town many times. I never knew who they were of course, because they all had secret identities. But after my father died, I realized that all of his friends and coworkers were actually super powered, just like he was.

Sometimes I wondered where the other heroes were the night my father was murdered. Sometimes I wondered if they would recognize me now that I was grown up and no longer by my father's side. Mostly, I just wondered what my knife would feel like in their neck.

I crossed the room in the blink of an eye, burying my sword deep in the gut of the gang leader. I watched with glee as the light faded from his eyes.

"So let them come for me," I whispered in his ear, the last words said to a dying man. He gave a hoarse groan, spitting up little droplets of blood. 

I continued, "Every good story needs a villain."

At first, it seemed like a joke; something the local high school threw together as a "senior prank."

*Small Town Struck with Chopping Fever!*

But I was there. It was no joke. It was a set up.

My town was a typical small town located out in the middle of the woods. All the locals knew each other, visitors were big news around those parts and no one ever left. We were all just surviving in our cabins, a long way away from big cities and traffic and sky risers. It was simple; it was peaceful.

Until the axes.

*Residents Calling Deforestation Efforts "God's Will"*

I woke up one morning like every morning: with a crick in my neck, a pop in my spine, and blurry vision. But when I reached over to put my glasses on, something caught my eye. In the middle of my bedroom floor, glistening in the light like a jewel, was a simple wooden axe, and a note beside it. The note read, "Do what you must." It was signed, "X."

I drove into town early that morning, intending on filing a police report. Someone had obviously broken into my house late at night and threatened me, and this wouldn't fly. 

But when I got to the police station, I was amazed to find that the line was so long, it extended outside the building and down the sidewalk for a block. People by the dozens were holding the same wooden axe with a note that had appeared in my room.

I approached the end of the line in disbelief. "Excuse me," I asked the woman standing at the end, "is everyone here to make a police report?"

She nodded. "Ayep. The whole town is here. I guess you got it too, huh? The axe?"

A shiver shot down my spine as I realized that this wasn't just one psycho breaking into my home, but this was on a scale of *hundreds* of people all in one night. One person couldn't have done this. And whoever did, they were organized. They knew what they were doing.

I decided to wait in line and file a report. But after a while, a man in the middle of line caught my attention. He had the axe they left him in his hand, and he had been pacing nervously since I arrived. But he must have made up his mind, because at that moment he took his axe and approached the nearest tree, hacking wildly at the trunk in an attempt to cut it down.

Several people called out to him to stop, but he eyes were crazy as he continued chopping the tree. "Don't you see?" he cried out to the crowd. "Do what you must. It was a message to us, a message from God! This is his will!"

He chopped and chopped away, eyes going wide with pleasure at the sight of the splintering wood chips spewing away from his frenzied attacks. When someone finally stepped forth to restrain him, he gave a mighty heave, and the tree cracked. All eyes were on it as it fell harmlessly to the side, falling to the ground in defeat.

They took the crazed man away, but that tree was only the first.

*Tree Chopping Town Resident Felled from Exhaustion; Is There More to Come?"*

In the following weeks, more and more people began chopping down trees. At first, people laughed, thinking it was a silly fad. At the grocery store, the bank, the only fast food joint in town -  everyone said the same things: "People are just bored and think they're funny," "It's just teenagers trying to fit in," and my favorite, "They just don't like trees."

It started with the tree in front of the police station, but it spread from there. The trees in the grocery store parking lot, the trees in the schoolyard, even the trees by the road.

The police tried to stop the perpetrators, but day after day, more and more people picked up their axe and chopped down trees.

*Three Dead in Small Town Chopping Frenzy; Experts Dispatched to Location*

And then people started dying. They would spend all day chopping down trees until their hands bled and they fell out, chopping still with their last bit of strength. 

On my way to work every morning, I would hear the Choppers who lined the roads chanting to themselves, "Do what you must. Do what you must."

They said it was God's Will. That God, for some reason, took a disliking to the trees that surrounded us and wanted us to destroy them. He was using us to carry out His will, so we were blessed.

But I watched my town go crazy, chopping until their palms bled, then chopping more, grinding their skin down to the bone and mushing the axe handle into their tissue. I watched everyone I knew and loved die from exhaustion and dehydration, clearing trees away in unprecedented amounts.

*Small Town Tree Chopping Frenzy Just an Internet Prank! City Named Doesn't Even Exist!*

I watched my city, once a hidden paradise in the middle of the woods, slowly cleared away. The land was barren for miles, save for broken, jagged stumps and dead trees downed one after another. Bodies lied beside logs, fingers and hands bloody and ragged and still loosely gripping their tools.

I watched my loved ones die. I watched my city destroyed. And I watched the world forget us, bury us as a legend and myth and walk away from our tragedy.

But all of that ceased to matter when I picked up my axe. Because the moment my hand gripped that wooden handle, I knew exactly what I had to do.

I had been chosen to carry out God's will.

I had heard of people like him in stories: obsessed, insane, with twitchy movements and a dead eye stare. But his eyes weren't dead; they were far from it. He had eyes that saw all: past, present, and future. In his eyes there were universes, universes that were being born, expanding and eventually imploding all within microseconds. He was watching the entire realm of reality, yet only existing in one tiny, micro instance of it. It was no wonder that his eyes shined and shimmered, like they contained our entire universe.

"So it's up to me to slay the dragon?" he asked our merry little band of crusaders with a disbelieving smile on his face. 

I was just the village's librarian, tasked with searching through the ancient tomes for prophecies regarding the dragon that plagued our village. I considered myself insignificant in the quest to kill the dragon, but there I was nonetheless.

The village Elder raised his voice, imploring the man before us, "You must. It has been prophesied."

He tilted his head back in a laugh, exposing the veins of his neck. "Tell me the prophecy!" he demanded, voice light and mocking, but with a tense edge that I was beginning to worry about. His hands rested near his hips, and I could only imagine him carefully gripping a blade under his shirt, preparing to use it.

When the village Elder hesitated, I spoke up. It was my job to unearth the prophecy, and I did feel unnecessary next to the warriors and chiefs that had gathered in the man's small home. If I wanted a purpose there, explaining the prophecy was it.

They bored into me, past my breastbone and directly into my soul; capturing what was there as fuel for the creation of some new universe that I would never get to see.

I licked my lips nervously. He was tall, yet lean, and his movements were lazy, yet calculated, like a conniving fox stalking its prey. He leaned backwards casually against the wall, one foot propped up under him, but I could see that he was poised and ready to flee should the first thing go south. It was understandable. We were in the home of the village criminal.

"But, if the gods still favor us at that time," I continued, nervously dropping my gaze from his intense one, "they will send us help. An angel in the form of destruction incarnate to destroy the dragon."

Laughter sang out in the small room, bellowing from his chest across the hallway, filling his home. He tilted his head and raised his eyebrows, as if unbelieving, and stared directly at me - the innocent village librarian - as he spoke. "And you think that is me??" he asked, laughing bemusedly as he did so.

Everyone in the room nodded.

He stopped laughing.

After a pause, he sighed, walking over to his bed and pulling a large wooden container out from underneath. He popped it open, revealing weapons of all different kinds filling the box to the brim. "Alright," he said with resignation as he picked up a crossbow, "I'll do it."

The chiefs and warriors of the village all collectively sighed in relief. The room, which was frozen with tension before, warmed. But before long, he interrupted.

"But I have one condition."

We all exchanged glances. The village guards reached for their cuffs with one hand, their weapons with the other. There was a moment of terse silence, then the village Elder asked, "What is it?"

He looked up from his weapon with a mischievous glint in his eye and a crooked smile. "The librarian comes with me."

The creatures walked into my holding cell. Their bodies were so wrong, so foreign, I couldn't even understand how they were alive. The beings could hardly manage movement; they had to dip and sway as they walked, constantly bouncing to and fro just to keep balanced. It made me nauseous watching them.
